opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I like to frame it is that LLMs have been this incredible success story for a particular kind of intelligence: language, symbolic reasoning, things that compress really well into one-dimensional sequences of tokens. And that's a huge part of what makes humans smart. But it's not all of it.

If you think about how animals, and humans before we ever had language, actually make their way through the world, so much of it is fundamentally spatial. You perceive a 3D world, you reason about where objects are, how they relate to each other, what happens if you push something or walk around a corner. You build a mental model of a space you've never fully seen, and then you act in it. That's a different kind of intelligence, and I don't think it falls out for free from scaling up next-token prediction on text.

So the open questions, to me, are things like: what's the right representation? Language is natively 1D, but the world is natively 3D, plus time. Do you want models that reason in pixels, in some latent 3D structure, in explicit geometry, or some mix? How do you get data at scale, given there's no "internet of 3D worlds" the way there's an internet of text? How do you go from perception, seeing a scene, to generation, building or imagining a consistent world, to interaction, actually acting inside it and having it respond?

And then how does that connect back to LLMs? I don't see it as a competition. I think the long-term picture is that these things fuse. Language is a great interface, a great way to express goals and abstractions, but grounding it in a rich spatial understanding of the world is what unlocks things like robotics, design, creative tools, AR, all these applications where you need to understand and manipulate actual 3D space. Right now we have systems that can talk beautifully about a room but can't really *see* it or build it in a coherent way, and closing that gap is the problem I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts LLMs’ language and symbolic reasoning with spatial intelligence, describing spatial understanding and action as a different kind of intelligence that does not follow automatically from scaling text prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that language models have gotten really, really good at a particular kind of intelligence, which is the kind that lives in text. And text is amazing, right? It's this compressed record of basically everything humans have ever bothered to write down. But there's a huge chunk of intelligence that never gets written down because it's just too obvious to us. Like, if I'm reaching for a coffee cup, I know where it is in three-dimensional space, I know how my hand needs to rotate, I know it's going to be heavy if it's full and light if it's empty. Nobody writes any of that down, because why would you? And so that whole chunk of understanding is kind of missing from the training data that LLMs see.

So the open question I keep coming back to is: can you get that for free out of language, or do you actually need a different kind of model? And my honest bet is that you need something different. Language is a one-dimensional sequence, and the world is three-dimensional and it changes over time, so it's really four-dimensional. You can describe 3D stuff with words, but it's lossy, and it's slow, and you lose the geometry. So I think of spatial intelligence as a parallel track to language. Not a replacement, not a plug-in, but its own foundational capability with its own representations and its own scaling story.

And then there are a few sub-questions underneath that. One is, what's the right representation? For language it's tokens, and that turned out to be a pretty good answer. For 3D we don't have a consensus yet. Is it point clouds, is it some kind of neural field, is it a video model that implicitly has geometry inside it? Nobody really knows, and I think that's one of the more exciting things right now, because whoever finds the "tokens for space" is going to unlock a lot.

The second one is data. Language had the internet. For spatial stuff, we have a lot of images and video, but we don't have a lot of data where the 3D structure is actually labeled. So you either get clever about extracting structure from 2D, or you generate a lot of your own data, or probably both.

And then the third one, which I think is the one people underrate, is what the model actually does once it has that understanding. With LLMs the output is text and that's fine, you read it. With spatial intelligence the output should be something you can walk into, or something a robot can act in, or something a designer can edit. So the interface question is just as hard as the modeling question. That's kind of the whole thesis for me: the next big wave isn't going to be a better chatbot, it's going to be models that actually understand the world the way we do, just by being in it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts language models’ text-based intelligence with spatial intelligence as a separate foundational capability grounded in 3D structure and interaction with the world.

astra-6.text:
I think the big question is: how much of the spatial structure of the world can you learn from language alone? Language contains a lot of information about the world, but it’s a particular kind of information. We don’t usually describe every geometric relationship in a scene, or every physical consequence of an action, because we take those things for granted.

So I’d separate two questions. One is whether an LLM can answer questions about space. The other is whether it has a representation that lets it reliably predict what happens when you move around, when an object moves, or when you interact with something. Those aren’t necessarily the same capability.

And then there’s the question of what’s missing. Do we just need to train these models on more images and video? Do they need experience taking actions and observing the consequences? Or do we need different architectures or training objectives that encourage a consistent model of the world?

I think those are still open questions. The interesting test is whether a model can use its understanding in a new situation—change the viewpoint, change the arrangement of objects, ask it to plan an interaction—and still get the relationships right.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts answering spatial questions with having a reliable spatial representation, but it does not mention or distinguish spatial intelligence from the intelligence represented by Dario’s “data center full of Einsteins.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big question is: what does it mean to understand space, and how much of that understanding can you get from language alone? An LLM can describe a room or tell you how to navigate somewhere, but that’s different from seeing an unfamiliar environment and knowing where things are, how they relate, and what would happen if you moved through it or interacted with something.

There are a few open questions there. What representations do you need? Do you need an explicit three-dimensional model, or can that structure emerge inside a model trained on images and video? What training signal gets you there—is observing the world enough, or does the system need to take actions and see the consequences?

And then there’s evaluation. How do we distinguish a model that has learned plausible things to say about space from one that can actually use spatial understanding in a new situation? I’d frame LLMs as a really powerful starting point, with an open question about what additional experience and structure they need.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes language-based capabilities from spatial understanding, but it does not identify or distinguish the intelligence represented by Dario’s “data center full of Einsteins.”
